proof: Emulators recreate a console so they can run its library. Static recompilation, the approach behind this toolkit, rebuilds one game at a time: the game's original CPU code is translated ahead of time into code compiled for modern systems, producing a native app. It trades broad compatibility for deeper control over rendering, input, networking, and game behavior. The two approaches complement each other, and this project builds on decades of knowledge from the emulation community.

A remaster is a new production. A source port needs source code or a long reverse-engineering effort for one title. An emulator reproduces the machine. Recompilation sits in its own spot: keep the original game logic, and swap the constraints around it.

items.text: Notebookcheck on Pepsiman in the browser

philosophy: Go native. Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, even the browser. No emulator core in sight.
See more of the world. Adaptive widescreen up to 21:9 in games like Tomba! 2 and Mega Man Zero.
Break the old limits. 60 FPS patches, CD-quality MSU-1 soundtracks, voxel 3D remixes, and mod loaders that never touch your original ROM.
Swap the hardware. Spin WarioWare: Twisted! with your phone or a DualSense, and let real local weather drive Boktai's solar sensor.
Change the words. Runtime text replacement powers Tsumu Light's English fan translation and NES text overrides.
Play together. Shared netplay, rollback, save states, and rewind (recomp-net and retcomm-rbengine) that every ecosystem can pick up.

pillars.title: Recompile
pillars.body: Translate the game's original CPU code ahead of time for modern systems.

pillars.title: Run
pillars.body: Provide the graphics, audio, input, storage, and other console services the game expects.

pillars.title: Extend
pillars.body: Add optional widescreen, modern controls, multiplayer, mods, translations, and other capabilities, where a project supports them.

transforms.title: Link cable becomes network play
transforms.body: Some PlayStation games connected two consoles with a serial cable. Reimplement that transport, and the same game logic can travel over a LAN or the internet while the game still believes it is talking to another console.

transforms.title: Fixed viewport becomes true widescreen
transforms.body: Understand how a game builds its camera and projection instead of stretching the final image. Demonstrated up to 21:9 in several projects.

transforms.title: Cartridge sensors become modern data
transforms.body: WarioWare: Twisted! reads a phone's gyroscope instead of its tilt cartridge. Boktai's solar sensor can be driven by real local weather.

transforms.title: Text becomes translatable, games become moddable
transforms.body: Runtime text replacement powers an English fan translation of Tsumu Light without patching the original image, and opt-in mod loaders never modify your dump.

transforms.title: One improvement can help many games
transforms.body: These transformations are built into the platform tooling, not into a single title. Once a display, input, or networking path exists for a platform, compatible games can often reuse it: every new game strengthens the tooling, and every platform improvement makes the next game easier.
